root_motivation: Grounding (2026-10-05 4:58pm PDT): the first real ownership email ever sent from prod reached Joe's Gmail and he judged it spammy on sight. origin/main's src/claim.rs carries three phishing-filter tells -- subject 'Claim your mcphost tenant', body 'Click to verify your email and finish claiming your mcphost tenant: {verify_url}', an imperative subject, sender claim@mcphost.dev with no display name -- and never states what happened or why this address got mail. Joe drafted and approved replacement copy (notes/drafts/mcphost-claim-copy-2026-10-05.md): the email states what an agent did and what the link does, the sender has a name, the claim-flow pages and error pages speak in the same voice, and no visible string says 'claim' or 'verify'.
user_persona: Three (PRD User stories): the stranger human who receives the ownership email and must trust it enough to click; the agent that relays skill step 5's sentence to its human; the operator (Joe) who diffs live strings against the approved draft file.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given a tenant named "my-agent" and a verify link, When the ownership email is rendered, Then its subject is `Your agent set up my-agent on mcphost — is this yours?` and its body equals the approved draft text with the placeholders filled, in plain text.
acceptance_criteria.test: tests/owncopy_ac01_email_subject_and_body_match_draft.rs -- fn ownership_email_subject_and_body_match_the_approved_draft drives signup+POST /claim/{token}, asserts the fake provider's captured subject/text_body against a hardcoded expectation copied from the draft.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given `MCPHOST_EMAIL_FROM="mcphost <hello@mcphost.dev>"`, When an email is sent through the fake provider, Then the request's `from` is that exact string and `reply_to` is `hello@mcphost.dev`.
acceptance_criteria.test: tests/owncopy_ac02_from_and_reply_to_passed_verbatim.rs -- fn from_is_passed_verbatim_and_reply_to_is_the_bare_address spawns the real `mcphost serve` binary with MCPHOST_EMAIL_FROM set in its environment (exercising EmailConfig::from_env()), asserts the request a local wiremock fake provider received has that from/reply_to.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given the three pages rendered with sample data, When their text is compared to the draft, Then titles, leads, button label, masked address, counts and closing lines match, and the done page shows the three "what owning it gives you" lines.
acceptance_criteria.test: tests/owncopy_ac03_pages_match_draft_text.rs -- fn the_three_pages_match_the_approved_draft GETs/POSTs the enter-address, after-send and done pages against a real published tool, asserting each draft substring.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given each of the seven error cases, When its page is rendered, Then the title and body are the draft's and no environment-variable name appears on the page.
acceptance_criteria.test: tests/owncopy_ac04_error_pages_match_draft_no_env_var.rs -- seven #[tokio::test]s, one per case (expired, already used, someone else first, mail not configured, rate limited, banned, send failed), each asserting the draft's title/body and the absence of any MCPHOST_ substring.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given the guard test over the email and every page, When it runs, Then no visible text contains `claim`, `verify` or `tenant` (case-insensitive) outside URLs and attributes.
acceptance_criteria.test: tests/owncopy_ac05_no_claim_verify_tenant_in_visible_text.rs -- fn no_visible_text_in_the_email_or_any_page_says_claim_verify_or_tenant renders the email and all ten pages (3 flow + 7 error), strips HTML tags (which drops attribute values with them) and skips URL-shaped tokens before scanning for the three forbidden words.

additional.state_line_format_fills_the_drafts_singl: The draft's What's here line reads '{calls}/{limit} calls this month · {state} of state' with one {state} placeholder, not {state_used}/{state_max}. Resolved by formatting {state} as 'state_bytes/state_bytes_max bytes' (symmetric with the calls fraction), rendering e.g. '0/5242880 bytes of state' -- no AC pins a different exact phrasing.
additional.upgrade_link_target_is_plans_html_not_an: The draft's done-page bullet 'choose a plan when the free tier stops being enough' 'links to upgrade', but the visitor on this page has no bearer key to call billing.checkout -- resolved by linking to the pre-existing /plans.html informational page (no price in its own heading either), not an authenticated checkout URL no unauthenticated page can mint.
additional.already_used_split_out_of_the_old_combin: ClaimVerifyOutcome already distinguishes NotFound/Expired/AlreadyConsumed at the DB layer, but the pre-existing code rendered all three identically. Resolved by keeping NotFound+Expired on the expired page (preserving resolve_claim_token's own never-leak-which-one-a-guess-was property -- AlreadyConsumed requires a code that was valid and already consumed, so splitting it out leaks nothing new) and giving AlreadyConsumed its own already-used page, matching the draft's two separate error-table rows.

five_whys_trace.q: Why did Joe judge the first real ownership email spammy on sight?
five_whys_trace.a: The subject was an imperative ('Claim your mcphost tenant') and the body opened with 'Click to verify your email' -- both classic phishing-filter tells, with a sender address (claim@mcphost.dev) carrying no display name.

five_whys_trace.q: Why did the shipped copy carry those tells?
five_whys_trace.a: It was written as a developer's description of the mechanism (claim a tenant, verify an email) rather than as a message to a person who never asked for mail and has no context for why they got it.

five_whys_trace.q: Why wasn't this caught before the first real send?
five_whys_trace.a: Every pre-existing test on the claim flow asserted the mechanism (a link exists, it sends once, it expires) never the literal copy a human would actually read.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does the wording matter this much for a flow that otherwise works end to end?
five_whys_trace.a: The human behind the agent is the market test's own weakest link (PRD problem statement); a recipient who deletes the email on sight never reaches the working flow at all, and a stranger with less context than Joe deletes faster.
